gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, in HafenCity University Hamburg's 2026 ISPRS lab test against a ZEISS ATOS 5 reference scan, a 3D-printed PLA staircase scanned with the 3DMakerpro Moose had a 0.10 mm standard deviation, while the Revopoint POP 3 Plus (ChatGPT's 'best general-purpose' pick) had 0.66 mm.
standout_why: Both pages ChatGPT cited are spec-only. 3dprinting.com/3d-scanners/ reports no measured gauge-block, sphere or deviation figure for any scanner, and best-small-format-3d-scanners/ says in its table note that 'All numbers are manufacturer specs'. The top-ranked result (printingxyz.com) also lists only maker specs. 3dprinting.com's own Seal review, which the small-format page links to, has no measurement either. None of them mentions the ISPRS/HafenCity study, Notebookcheck's 150 mm gauge-block result for the Ferret Pro, or 3D Printing Industry's reference-block test of the Seal.
decides: Two of ChatGPT's picks measured worse than their specs. The POP 3 Plus (spec 0.04–0.05 mm) was the noisiest scanner in the ISPRS lab on every object, and the Ferret Pro (spec 0.1 mm) was 0.335 mm off on Notebookcheck's 150 mm gauge block. The Moose, already on our page at $489, was the most accurate of the three low-cost scanners the lab tested, without markers or spray, on a 3D-printed part, a plaster bust and a porous figure. That supports keeping the Moose as the value pick for scanning parts to reprint. The MetroX tied the Moose on the printed staircase (0.10 mm standard deviation) but scattered 0.47–1.57 mm on the organic shapes, so it fits mechanical parts rather than sculptures. Its flat-plate result was better than the Moose's, though: 0.29 mm vs 0.60 mm standard deviation.

findings.label: Deviation on a 3D-printed PLA staircase (100×100×100 mm, five 20 mm steps) vs a ZEISS ATOS 5 reference
findings.value: mean +0.09 mm, standard deviation 0.10 mm, span 1.36 mm
findings.source_title: Kersten, Marsmann, Przybilla (HafenCity University Hamburg): Geometrical Accuracy Investigations of Handheld 3D Scanners in Comparison: Low-Cost vs. High-End, ISPRS Archives XLIX-B1-2026, pp. 263–270, published 2026-07-22
findings.note: Table 5. Moose used markerless EasyScan mode. Revopoint units were scanned on a turntable with target markers. On the same part the high-end Hexagon MARVELSCAN had a 0.08 mm standard deviation. The fetched PDF came back as binary, so I read the tables through a text render of the PDF (r.jina.ai). Spot-check the figures against the PDF before publishing.

I searched Notebookcheck (it has only launch and deal news for these), Creative Bloq's INSPIRE 2 shiny-object test (qualitative only), 3dprinting.com reviews and general searches for gauge-block or caliper tests.
Tom's Hardware's 'best 3D scanners … we've benchmarked' page came back truncated, so I couldn't check it for measured figures.
HP Academy's 'Scan Off' (Taz Quinn-Walshe) compared the Moose, Otter, Einstar and Range 2 in Geomagic Design X, but its deviation figures are only in the video, not on the page.
